text: Oh no, wild [[qubit|Qubits]] have found us! Let's understand our enemy before we defend ourselves.
See that strange [[ket|| ⟩ notation]]? That just holds the state of the qubit. If a dangerous [[basis||0⟩]] slips past our defenses, we lose HP!
Every qubit can be pictured as an arrow on the [[bloch|Bloch sphere]]. |0⟩ points to the north pole, |1⟩ to the south pole, and every other state points somewhere in between.

bloch.caption: Arrow at the top: dangerous |0⟩. Arrow at the bottom: harmless |1⟩.

text: Our goal is to flip them into harmless |1⟩ states so we don't take damage.
Grab the [[x|X flipper]] from the top bar! It magically flips a |0⟩ into a |1⟩ as the enemy passes through.
On the Bloch sphere, the X flipper is a half turn around the x-axis (the gold dashed line). Watch the arrow swing from the north pole |0⟩ all the way down to the south pole |1⟩.
Flippers aren't free. Your coins are in the top-left, and each flipper's cost is shown under its symbol. You can't place one you can't afford, and right-clicking a placed flipper refunds it.
Survive with any HP left and the next level unlocks. Spend no more than the level's optimal cost and you also earn a ★. Your stars show up on the level select screen.
Click a grid line to place your X flipper. Right-click if you want to remove it. Press ▶ when you're ready!
↶ undoes your last move, ⟲ clears the board, and the slider in the bottom-left sets the speed. ▶ (or Space) launches the qubits, and pressing it again pauses them.

These notes stay in the box at the bottom: page through them with ‹ ›, or reopen this window with ⤢. Underlined words like [[qubit|qubit]] open the Ψ encyclopedia (top-right), which collects every new term you meet.
Placed! Every qubit that crosses that line passes through your X flipper. Press ▶ (or Space) when you're ready.
There it goes! The flipper turned the arrow from |0⟩ to |1⟩. Look at the qubit's numbers: the 1 and the 0 swapped places.
Ouch! A |0⟩ reached our base. Its P(0) was 1, so it hit us for the full 100 HP. Retry, and put an X flipper in its path first.
Perfect! A gate acts on every qubit that passes through it, so one well-placed gate can handle a whole lane.
You survived! But what was that HP system about? When a qubit hits the left edge, we [[measurement|'measure']] it. Measurement forces it to [[collapse|collapse]] into either |0⟩ or |1⟩.
The [[amplitude|top number α]] tells us how likely it is to collapse to |0⟩ — specifically, it's |α|² (alpha squared). A pure |0⟩ means α=1, so P(0)=100% and we take 100 damage!
This |α|² rule is called [[born|Born's Rule]], one of the foundations of quantum mechanics. Our HP loss is just the expected damage from that random collapse.
Those flippers you used? In quantum mechanics, they are actually called [[gate|'gates']].
Place an X gate in lane 1 and watch the numbers! X swaps the top and bottom: 1|0⟩+0|1⟩ becomes 0|0⟩+1|1⟩. The top goes to 0 so no damage!
Now try a [[y|Y gate]] in lane 2. Y also swaps the amplitudes, but multiplies them by [[imaginary|-i and i]]. The output looks different, but the top is still 0... so damage is still 0!
Try the [[z|Z gate]] in lane 3, then press ▶ and keep an eye on that qubit's numbers as it passes through.
Z multiplies only the bottom amplitude by -1. Watch the numbers change... but notice the top amplitude stays the same. Damage is unchanged!

bloch.caption: Z: half turn around the vertical z-axis. |+⟩ becomes |−⟩, but the arrow stays on the equator, exactly as far from |0⟩ as before.

text: So X and Y both block damage, while Z seems useless for now. But Z did change the numbers! That -1 will matter a lot in the next level. For now, use X and Y to survive!
Y left an i on the bottom where X left a 1. |i|² = 1, so the qubit is just as harmless. Different numbers, same damage.

Ouch! Each qubit that reaches the base hits for P(0) × 100, so a |0⟩ costs the full 100. The lane 3 qubit, 1/√2|0⟩ + 1/√2|1⟩, has P(0) = |1/√2|² = ½, so it costs 50, and none of your gates can stop that one yet.
You survived! X and Y blocked the |0⟩ enemies completely. Z changed the numbers but not the damage. Remember that -1 twist — it won't always be useless.
Remember that -1 twist from Z that didn't help last time? This level is why it exists.

Your new enemies are in [[superposition|state 1/√2|0⟩ + 1/√2|1⟩]]. The top and bottom are equal, so there's a 50% chance of |0⟩. Each one that slips through costs 50 HP, and two come down every lane, so you can't afford to leave a lane undefended.
You have an [[h|H gate]]! H is special — it mixes the top and bottom amplitudes together. Try placing just an H and see what happens...
Ouch! If you tried a lone H, look at what it did: it turned 1/√2|0⟩ + 1/√2|1⟩ into a pure |0⟩. That's 100 damage, even worse than doing nothing!

bloch.caption: H takes |+⟩ straight to the north pole: a pure, dangerous |0⟩.

text: Why? H adds the two amplitudes together, and 1/√2 + 1/√2 reinforce each other into a full 1 on top. H amplified the |0⟩. We need to break that reinforcement.
Now add a Z gate to the right of your H gate (so qubits hit Z first). Z flips the bottom to -1/√2. Now H sees +1/√2 and -1/√2 — they cancel out! The |0⟩ vanishes. Zero damage!
Z flipped the bottom to −1/√2. Now when H adds the two amplitudes, +1/√2 and −1/√2 cancel out.

You used [[interference|quantum interference]]! When two amplitudes with opposite signs meet, they cancel. Z set up the cancellation, and H triggered it. This is the secret inside every quantum computer.
You've seen that Z sets up the -1/√2 that lets H cancel the |0⟩ away. But what if the -1 is already there from the start?
Look carefully at your enemies this time. Some have a + on the bottom, some have a -. That sign changes everything!
The ones with + at the bottom are [[plusminus||+⟩]]. They need Z first, then H — just like last level.
The ones with - at the bottom are |−⟩. They already have the right setup! H alone will turn them into a perfect |1⟩ — zero damage!
Spot the sign in each lane, then place the right combination. One set of gates per lane!
Ouch! Check the sign in each lane. Z then H only works on |+⟩. On a |−⟩, the Z flips it back to |+⟩, and H sends that straight to |0⟩.

Brilliant! The sign on the bottom number told you everything. Signs like this — which physicists call [[phase|'phases']] — are invisible to measurement, but H turns them into real differences in outcome. This is quantum interference at work.
Time to use everything you've learned! All four gates — X, Y, Z, and H — are in your arsenal.

The first two lanes have identical |0⟩ enemies. Both X and Y can fix them! Try putting X in one lane and Y in the other — watch how the numbers after each gate are different, even though the damage is the same.
The third lane has |+⟩ enemies — equal + signs on both numbers. You know the Z+H trick: Z flips the bottom negative so H can cancel the |0⟩ away.
The fourth lane has |−⟩ enemies — the ones with the minus sign on the bottom. H alone turns them straight into |1⟩.
One gate per lane where you can, combine where you must. You've got this!
Compare the first two lanes: X leaves a 1 on the bottom, Y leaves an i. Different numbers, but |i|² = 1, so both are equally harmless.
Ouch! Read each lane's numbers before you pick: |0⟩ needs a flip, |+⟩ needs Z then H, and |−⟩ needs only H.

You've mastered the core toolkit! X and Y both flip |0⟩ to |1⟩, but leave different numbers behind. H creates and resolves superposition, and Z sets up the interference that H needs. Every one of these gates is [[unitary|unitary]]: reversible, and it never changes the total probability. They can't build everything on their own, though. Finer turns are next.
New gate: the [[s|S gate]]! S multiplies the bottom amplitude by i. On the Bloch sphere, that's a quarter turn (90°) around the vertical axis.
Two quarter turns make a half turn, so S followed by S is exactly a Z. That's why S is sometimes written √Z.

bloch.caption: S, then S: two quarter turns land on |−⟩, exactly where a single Z would.

text: Look at lane 1: 1/√2|0⟩ + i/√2|1⟩. That's |+i⟩, on the sphere's y-axis. H alone can't fix it: H swaps the x and z axes, and leaves y-axis states stuck on the equator.
But one S turns |+i⟩ into |−⟩, and you already know H turns |−⟩ into |1⟩. Put the S first (further right), then the H.
Lane 2 is |−i⟩, on the opposite side. A quarter turn takes it the wrong way... how many quarter turns does it need? Could a gate you already know do some of that turning for less?
Watch the bottom number: S multiplied it by i. The probabilities didn't change. The arrow just slid 90° around the equator.
Ouch! Remember: H only lands on |1⟩ from |−⟩. Count the quarter turns each lane needs to get there.
Quarter turns mastered! S slides states 90° around the equator, and S + S = Z. Next: an even finer turn.
Meet the [[t|T gate]]: an eighth of a turn (45°) around the vertical axis. It multiplies the bottom amplitude by e^{iπ/4} = (1+i)/√2.
T + T = S, and S + S = Z. Every [[p|phase gate]] is the same kind of turn, just bigger or smaller.

bloch.caption: T, then T: two eighth turns make the quarter turn of a single S.

text: These swarms sit on the equator at 45° steps. The goal hasn't changed: turn each one until it reaches |−⟩ (180° round from |+⟩), then let H drop it to |1⟩.
Count the degrees: lane 1 starts 45° round and needs 135° more. Lane 2 starts at 135° and needs just 45°. Mix T and S to land exactly on 180°.
Close isn't good enough here. An arrow 45° off still has about a 15% chance of collapsing to |0⟩, and there are a lot of qubits coming.
That T nudged the arrow 45° round the equator. Its bottom number turned with it, multiplied by (1+i)/√2, while the top number stayed put.
Ouch! Even a 45° error adds up across a whole swarm. Check that each lane turns by exactly the right amount.

Precision achieved! T is the smallest turn in your toolkit, and a special one: circuits built only from H, S and CNOT can be simulated efficiently on an ordinary computer. Adding T is what makes them truly quantum.
Sandbox time! Every single-qubit gate you've met is available, plus the [[i|Identity gate]] I, which does absolutely nothing. Whether that's worth a coin is up to you.
Space is tight: each lane only has room for three gates. Plan each lane as a short chain of turns that ends exactly at |1⟩.
Tip: on the equator, X and Y act like mirrors. X sends a phase of φ to −φ, and Y sends it to 180° − φ. A mirror can be cheaper than a long chain of turns.

bloch.caption: X mirrors the arrow across the x-axis: 225° becomes 135°.

text: Lane 1 is a swarm again, so close isn't good enough there. Lanes 2 and 3 should look familiar.
The I gate did... absolutely nothing. Exactly as advertised. It still took a coin and a slot, so make sure it's earning them.
Ouch! Every lane has to end at exactly |1⟩. Lane 1 is a swarm, so even 45° off leaks about 15% of a hit per qubit, many times over.

Single-qubit master! Every single-qubit gate is a rotation of the Bloch sphere, and H and T together can get as close as you like to any rotation. Add a two-qubit gate and you have a [[universal|universal gate set]]. Time to bring in a second qubit...
These qubits arrive [[entanglement|entangled]]. Each glowing pair shares a single state, 1/√2|00⟩ + 1/√2|11⟩, called a [[bell|Bell state]]. Measure one qubit and you instantly know the other.

Entangled qubits have no amplitudes of their own, so they show P(1), the chance that each one is harmless. Here it's 1/2, and no single-qubit gate can change that. Hover over a pair to see their shared state.
Enter the [[cnot|CNOT gate]]! It sits on a corner between two lanes. When a qubit crosses it in each lane at the same moment, it flips the target (⊕) if the control (●) is |1⟩.
Run a Bell pair through a CNOT and the entanglement unravels: 1/√2|00⟩ + 1/√2|11⟩ becomes |+⟩ on the control and |0⟩ on the target. Finish them off with gates you already know.

Click a placed CNOT to swap control and target. And watch out for the straggler: a controlled gate only works on two qubits crossing it together. A lone qubit passes straight through, as if the gate weren't there.
The pair split up! Their colour faded back to purple: each qubit has its own state again, so your single-qubit gates work on it.

Ouch! Check what reached the base. A lone qubit crosses the CNOT as if it weren't there, so it needs single-qubit gates. A pair that went through the CNOT leaves |+⟩ on the control and |0⟩ on the target, and each needs its own fix.
You made a new pair! A CNOT whose control is in superposition creates entanglement, the opposite of what you want here. Check the order of your gates.
Spooky action, handled. CNOT can create entanglement as easily as it removes it: feed it |+⟩ and |0⟩ and out comes the very Bell pair you just fought.

Entanglement sandbox! Bell pairs come in four flavours: Φ+ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, Φ− = (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2, Ψ+ = (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 and Ψ− = (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2. Hover over a pair to see which one you're facing.
Pairs can span lanes 1–2 or lanes 2–3, and lone superpositions slip through in between. A corner gate only fires for qubits that cross it together, so the lone ones pass straight through.
Single-qubit gates alone can never change an entangled qubit's P(1). A CNOT has to do the untangling. But a well-chosen gate before the CNOT can decide what comes out of it...
Hint: CNOT followed by H on the control turns Ψ− straight into |11⟩. Which cheap gates turn your other pairs into a Ψ−?

bloch.caption: Ψ− through a CNOT leaves |−⟩ on the control and |1⟩ on the target. One H later, both are harmless.

text: Untangled! Each qubit has its own amplitudes again. Hover over them to see which state each one is in before it reaches the base.
Ouch! A CNOT and an H on the control unravel any Bell pair, but what comes out depends on which pair it was. Hover over each pair, then fix the leftovers with single-qubit gates.
Every Bell pair can be unravelled with a CNOT and an H. That's exactly how quantum computers read out entanglement, in a step called a [[bellmeasurement|Bell measurement]].
These pairs are tangled through their phase: (|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩ − |11⟩)/2. Every outcome is equally likely. Only the minus sign on |11⟩ ties them together.
Meet the [[cz|CZ gate]]: it flips the sign of |11⟩ and nothing else. Run this pair through it and the minus sign disappears, leaving two independent |+⟩ qubits.
CZ is symmetric: there's no control or target, so there's nothing to flip. Once the qubits are free, you know how to take |+⟩ to |1⟩.
Untangled! The minus sign is gone, and each qubit is a plain |+⟩ again.
CZ is a CNOT in disguise: put an H on each side of the target and a CZ behaves exactly like a CNOT.
This pair carries an imaginary twist: 1/√2|00⟩ + i/√2|11⟩. That i is a phase, so you can't see it in the probabilities, but it decides how the pair unravels.
Meet the [[cy|CY gate]]: if the control (●) is |1⟩, it applies Y to the target. Y brings its own factor of ±i, which can cancel the pair's i exactly.
Like CNOT, CY has a direction: click a placed CY to swap control and target. Try both ways, and watch which lane ends up in which state. The cheapest answer isn't the obvious one.
Untangled! The i got absorbed by the Y. Hover over the qubits to see where each one ended up.
Controlled-anything: any single-qubit gate can be given a control qubit. CNOT, CZ and CY are just the three most famous.
These Ψ− pairs have split up: one qubit in lane 1, its partner in lane 3. A corner gate only joins neighbouring lanes, so no CNOT can reach both halves.
Meet the [[swap|SWAP gate]]: it trades the states of the two qubits crossing its corner. The harmless |1⟩ in lane 2 makes a perfect stand-in to swap with.
Bring each pair together, then remember the trick from the Entanglement Sandbox: CNOT followed by H on the control turns Ψ− straight into |11⟩.
Swapped! The two qubits traded lanes, and the entanglement moved with them. The pair's halves are now neighbours.
Untangled! Each qubit has its own state again. Finish each one off on its way to the base.
SWAP carries entanglement with it: the pair stays exactly as tangled, it just changes lanes. A SWAP is three CNOTs in a row, which is why it costs more than one.
The full controlled-gate suite is yours: CX (the same gate as CNOT, under its other common name), CY and CZ. Three different pairs are coming, one after another, down lanes 1–2, 2–3 and 3–4.

Each pair is tangled in its own way. Lanes 1–2 bring a plain Bell pair, (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2. Lanes 2–3 bring a pair tied together only by a minus sign. Lanes 3–4 bring one carrying an i. Hover over each to read its state.
Match the tool to the tangle: CX for the plain Bell pair, CZ for the pair joined by a sign, and CY for the one with an i, just like the levels where you met them.
The catch: lanes 2 and 3 each carry qubits from two different pairs, so a single-qubit gate there hits both. And with only four columns, every gate has to earn its place.
One pair down! Hover over the freed qubits to check they're heading for |1⟩.
Ouch! Lanes 2 and 3 carry qubits from two different pairs, so every gate there hits both. Look for gates that do the right thing to each.
Suite complete! CX, CY and CZ differ only by single-qubit gates around the target. Once you have one [[controlled|controlled gate]] and single-qubit gates, you can build all the others.

Trouble: this pair, 1/√2|00⟩ + (−1+i)/2|11⟩, is split across lanes 1 and 3, and a harmless |1⟩ sits between them. Corner gates only join neighbours, so the pair needs [[routing|routing]] before you can untangle it.
That (−1+i)/2 hides a phase of 135°, three eighth-turns. After everything you've seen, you know which gate deals in eighth-turns.
Here's a trick: that harmless |1⟩ in lane 2 is more than a bystander. Used as a control, it's always 'on', so a controlled gate across its corner always fires on the neighbour.
Lanes 2 and 3 get more harmless |1⟩s later, and lane 1 a lone |+⟩. Whatever you place in a lane, every qubit in it passes through, so keep the bystanders safe.
Routed and untangled! Every qubit is on its own again.
Ouch! Check the bystanders: every qubit in a lane passes through every gate in it, so the harmless |1⟩s and the lone |+⟩ have to come out as |1⟩ too.
Real quantum chips face this exact problem: qubits only talk to their neighbours, so compilers spend a lot of effort deciding where to route qubits, and when a neighbour can do the job instead.
A [[ghz|GHZ state]]: three qubits tangled at once, 1/√2|000⟩ + (−1+i)/2|111⟩. Measure any one of them and the other two instantly follow.
You can't untangle three qubits with one gate, but you can peel them apart one at a time. A CX from one GHZ qubit onto another sets the target free and leaves a Bell pair behind.

bloch.caption: CX on the first two qubits of a GHZ triad: the target's arrow grows back to full length (it's free), while the other two stay entangled as a Bell pair.

text: More arrivals follow: lone qubits, then two smaller pairs, one of them carrying the same 135° phase. Gates on a lane hit every qubit that passes, so look for a layout that works for all of them.
A qubit broke free! Keep peeling.
Ouch! Every gate on a lane hits each qubit that passes, whichever group it belongs to. Find a layout that works for the triad, the lone qubits and both pairs.
GHZ states are named after Greenberger, Horne and Zeilinger, who showed that three entangled qubits break the classical picture of the world even more dramatically than two do.
